hook.text: You open Instagram. In 200 milliseconds, dozens of services collaborate to show your feed.

buildup.text: System design is the art of deciding how software components connect and work together.

discovery.text: It answers questions like: where does data live, how do parts communicate, what happens at scale?

twist.text: There's no single correct design. Every choice involves trade-offs between competing goals.

climax.text: Great system design isn't about perfection — it's about making the right trade-offs for your context.

punchline.text: Design is choosing which trade-offs you can live with.

quiz.question: What is system design fundamentally about?
options: How software components connect and work together

hook.text: A startup's prototype works for 100 users. At 100,000 users, everything collapses.

buildup.text: Code quality alone can't save you. Architecture determines whether a system survives growth.

discovery.text: System design decides cost, speed, reliability, and how fast your team can ship features.

twist.text: The biggest tech companies spend more time on design than on writing code.

climax.text: Good design lets a small team serve millions. Bad design buries a large team in chaos.

punchline.text: Architecture decides if your system scales or breaks.

quiz.question: Why do big tech companies spend more time on design than coding?
options: Architecture determines if a system survives growth

hook.text: A chat app must send messages. That's functional. It must send them in under 100ms. That's non-functional.

buildup.text: Functional requirements define what the system does. Non-functional define how well it does it.

discovery.text: Latency, throughput, availability, and durability are the big four non-functional requirements.

twist.text: Teams often nail the functional requirements but ignore the non-functional ones until production breaks.

climax.text: Non-functional requirements are invisible until they fail — then they're the only thing anyone notices.

punchline.text: Users notice speed and uptime, not features.

quiz.question: What is a non-functional requirement?
options: How well the system performs, like latency and availability

hook.text: How much storage does YouTube need per day? A quick napkin calculation gives you the answer.

buildup.text: Back-of-the-envelope math estimates scale: users × actions × data size × time.

discovery.text: 500 hours of video uploaded per minute × 1 GB/hour ≈ 720 TB per day. That shapes the design.

twist.text: You don't need exact numbers. The goal is order of magnitude — megabytes vs terabytes vs petabytes.

climax.text: Estimation reveals whether your design is feasible before you write a single line of code.

punchline.text: Napkin math prevents million-dollar mistakes.

quiz.question: What is the goal of back-of-the-envelope estimation?
options: Determine order of magnitude to check feasibility

topics.title: The Anatomy of a Web Request

hook.text: You type a URL and press Enter. In 300 milliseconds, a page appears. What happened in between?

buildup.text: DNS resolves the domain. Your browser opens a TCP connection and sends an HTTP request.

discovery.text: A load balancer routes you to one of many servers. The server queries a database and returns HTML.

twist.text: CDN caches, TLS handshakes, and connection pooling all happen invisibly to make it feel instant.

climax.text: A single web request touches DNS, load balancers, servers, databases, and caches — in milliseconds.

punchline.text: One click triggers a dozen systems in 300ms.

quiz.question: What is the first step when you type a URL?
options: DNS resolves the domain name to an IP address

hook.text: Every time you use an app, your device is the client and a remote machine is the server.

buildup.text: Clients request data. Servers process requests and send responses. This is client-server architecture.

discovery.text: A single server can handle thousands of clients simultaneously using connection multiplexing.

twist.text: Modern apps blur the line. Peer-to-peer systems like BitTorrent make every device both client and server.

climax.text: Client-server is the foundation of nearly every internet service, from email to streaming.

punchline.text: One asks, one answers — the web's oldest pattern.

quiz.question: What does a server do in client-server architecture?

hook.text: One server handles 1,000 requests per second. You need to handle 50,000. What do you do?

buildup.text: A load balancer sits in front of multiple servers and distributes incoming requests across them.

discovery.text: Round-robin, least connections, and weighted algorithms decide which server gets each request.

twist.text: Load balancers also detect unhealthy servers and stop sending traffic to them automatically.

climax.text: Without load balancers, scaling horizontally would be impossible. They're the traffic cops of the internet.

punchline.text: Split the traffic, multiply the capacity.

quiz.question: What does a load balancer do?

hook.text: Servers are stateless — they forget everything after each request. Databases remember.

buildup.text: Databases store data durably so it survives server restarts, crashes, and deployments.

discovery.text: Relational databases use tables and SQL. NoSQL databases use documents, key-value pairs, or graphs.

twist.text: Choosing the wrong database for your workload is one of the hardest mistakes to fix later.

climax.text: The database is the heart of most systems. Everything else can be replaced more easily.

punchline.text: Pick the right database — it's the hardest to change.

quiz.question: Why is the database choice so critical?
options: It's the hardest component to replace later

hook.text: Reading from a database takes 5 milliseconds. Reading from cache takes 0.1 milliseconds. That's 50x faster.

buildup.text: A cache stores frequently accessed data in fast memory so the database isn't hit every time.

discovery.text: Redis and Memcached are popular caches. They sit between the application and the database.

twist.text: Cache invalidation — knowing when cached data is stale — is famously one of the hardest problems in computing.

climax.text: Caching is the single most effective way to make a slow system fast.

punchline.text: The fastest query is the one you don't make.

quiz.question: What is cache invalidation?
options: Knowing when cached data is stale and needs refreshing

hook.text: You upload a video to YouTube. It takes minutes to process, but the upload response is instant.

buildup.text: A message queue accepts the task, stores it, and a background worker processes it later.

discovery.text: Kafka, RabbitMQ, and SQS decouple producers from consumers so neither has to wait for the other.

twist.text: If a worker crashes mid-task, the queue retries automatically. Messages survive failures.

climax.text: Message queues turn synchronous bottlenecks into asynchronous, resilient pipelines.

punchline.text: Don't wait — queue it and process later.

quiz.question: Why are message queues useful?
options: They decouple producers from consumers for async processing

hook.text: You post a photo. Your friend in Tokyo doesn't see it for 10 seconds. Is that a bug?

buildup.text: Consistency means everyone sees the same data at the same time. Availability means the system always responds.

discovery.text: The CAP theorem says during a network partition, you must choose consistency or availability — not both.

twist.text: Banks choose consistency — your balance must be correct. Social media chooses availability — a slight delay is fine.

climax.text: There's no universal answer. The right choice depends on what your users can tolerate.

punchline.text: Correct or always-on — pick one during failures.

quiz.question: What does the CAP theorem state?
options: During a partition, you must choose consistency or availability
All three guarantees are always possible

hook.text: A highway can move 10,000 cars per hour but each car takes 30 minutes. That's high throughput, high latency.

buildup.text: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests the system handles per second.

discovery.text: Batching improves throughput but increases latency. Processing one at a time is fast but low throughput.

twist.text: Optimizing for one often hurts the other. A system tuned for real-time chat differs from one for batch ETL.

climax.text: Great system design balances latency and throughput based on what users actually need.

punchline.text: Fast per request or fast in bulk — rarely both.

quiz.question: What is throughput?
options: How many requests a system handles per second

hook.text: Your server is maxed out. Do you buy a bigger machine or add more machines?

buildup.text: Vertical scaling means upgrading to a more powerful server. Horizontal scaling means adding more servers.

discovery.text: Vertical is simpler but has a ceiling — the biggest machine in the world still has limits.

twist.text: Horizontal scaling is theoretically unlimited but requires load balancing, data partitioning, and coordination.

climax.text: Most large systems use both: scale up as far as practical, then scale out.

punchline.text: Scale up until you can't, then scale out.

quiz.question: What is horizontal scaling?
options: Adding more servers to handle load
Upgrading to a more powerful server
Adding more RAM to one machine

hook.text: SQL databases enforce strict schemas. NoSQL databases let you store anything in any shape.

buildup.text: SQL excels at complex queries, joins, and transactions. NoSQL excels at scale and flexibility.

discovery.text: SQL databases scale vertically well. NoSQL databases are designed to scale horizontally from day one.

twist.text: Modern SQL databases like CockroachDB scale horizontally. NoSQL databases like MongoDB added transactions.

climax.text: The boundary between SQL and NoSQL is blurring. Choose based on your access patterns, not hype.

punchline.text: Pick the database that fits your queries, not trends.

quiz.question: What is a key advantage of NoSQL databases?
options: Designed to scale horizontally from day one

hook.text: A monolith puts everything in one process. A distributed system spreads work across many machines.

buildup.text: Monoliths are simple to build, test, and deploy. One codebase, one deployment, one database.

discovery.text: Distributed systems handle more load but add complexity: network failures, data sync, and debugging.

twist.text: Many successful companies ran monoliths for years. Shopify still runs one serving billions in commerce.

climax.text: Distribution is a tool, not a goal. Add complexity only when the monolith can no longer cope.

punchline.text: Start simple. Distribute when you must.

quiz.question: When should you move from a monolith to a distributed system?
options: When the monolith can no longer handle the load
From the very start of every project

hook.text: Almost every app you use talks to servers through REST APIs. They're the lingua franca of the web.

buildup.text: REST uses HTTP verbs — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE — to perform operations on resources.

discovery.text: Each resource has a URL. GET /users/42 retrieves user 42. DELETE /users/42 removes them.

twist.text: REST is simple but can be chatty. Fetching a complex page might require dozens of separate API calls.

climax.text: REST's simplicity made it the default. Its limitations spawned GraphQL and gRPC.

punchline.text: Simple, universal, and good enough for most systems.

quiz.question: What HTTP verb retrieves a resource in REST?

hook.text: A phone call is synchronous — both sides must be present. A text message is asynchronous.

buildup.text: Sync communication blocks the caller until the response arrives. Async lets the caller continue working.

discovery.text: HTTP requests are synchronous. Message queues and event buses enable asynchronous communication.

twist.text: Async is faster but harder to debug. When something fails, tracing the chain of events is complex.

climax.text: Most systems use both: sync for user-facing calls, async for background processing.

punchline.text: Sync for answers now, async for work later.

quiz.question: What is an example of asynchronous communication?

hook.text: In a chat app, messages appear instantly without refreshing. That's WebSockets, not regular HTTP.

buildup.text: HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. WebSockets keep a persistent connection open.

discovery.text: Once connected, either side can send data at any time. This enables real-time chat, gaming, and dashboards.

twist.text: WebSocket connections consume server memory. At millions of connections, the cost adds up fast.

climax.text: WebSockets trade efficiency for immediacy — essential for real-time, overkill for everything else.

punchline.text: A connection that stays open for instant data.

quiz.question: How do WebSockets differ from HTTP?
options: They keep a persistent two-way connection open

topics.title: GraphQL: Ask for Exactly What You Need

hook.text: A REST API returns 50 fields when you only need 3. GraphQL lets you request exactly those 3.

buildup.text: GraphQL uses a single endpoint where clients specify the exact shape of data they want.

discovery.text: Facebook created GraphQL in 2012 to solve the problem of mobile apps over-fetching data.

twist.text: GraphQL reduces over-fetching but adds complexity: caching is harder and queries can be expensive.

climax.text: GraphQL shines when clients have diverse data needs. REST is simpler when they don't.

punchline.text: One query, exactly the data you need.

quiz.question: What problem did GraphQL originally solve?
options: Mobile apps over-fetching data from REST APIs

hook.text: REST sends data as human-readable JSON. gRPC sends compact binary — up to 10x smaller and faster.

buildup.text: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to serialize data into tiny binary payloads with strict schemas.

discovery.text: It supports streaming, bidirectional communication, and auto-generated client libraries in any language.

twist.text: gRPC isn't browser-friendly. It's dominant for service-to-service calls but rare for public APIs.

climax.text: gRPC is the go-to for internal microservice communication where speed and type safety matter most.

punchline.text: Binary beats JSON when machines talk to machines.

quiz.question: When is gRPC most commonly used?

hook.text: Twitter has 500 million tweet reads per second but only 6,000 new tweets per second. That's read-heavy.

buildup.text: Read-heavy systems optimize for fast retrieval: caching, replicas, and denormalized data.

discovery.text: Write-heavy systems like logging platforms optimize for fast ingestion: append-only logs and batch writes.

twist.text: The same data can be in both: write-optimized for ingestion, then transformed into a read-optimized view.

climax.text: Understanding your read/write ratio is the first step in designing the right data architecture.

punchline.text: Know your ratio — it shapes every decision.

quiz.question: What characterizes a read-heavy system?
options: Far more data reads than writes

hook.text: If your only database server dies, all your data is gone. Replication keeps copies on multiple machines.

buildup.text: A primary database handles writes and replicates changes to one or more read replicas.

discovery.text: Replicas serve read traffic, reducing load on the primary and surviving if one machine fails.

twist.text: Replication lag means replicas might serve slightly stale data. Seconds matter in financial systems.

climax.text: Replication trades perfect consistency for durability and read performance.

punchline.text: Copies protect data and speed up reads.

quiz.question: What is replication lag?
options: Delay before replicas reflect the latest writes
Time to create a new replica

hook.text: One database holds 10 TB. Queries are slow. Splitting it across 10 machines makes each one fast again.

buildup.text: Sharding splits data into partitions. Each shard holds a subset, like users A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2.

discovery.text: A good shard key distributes data evenly. A bad one creates hot spots that overload one shard.

twist.text: Cross-shard queries are expensive. If user A's data needs user B's data on another shard, joins get complex.

climax.text: Sharding enables massive scale but adds complexity in routing, rebalancing, and cross-shard operations.

punchline.text: Split data to scale — but choose the split wisely.

quiz.question: What is a hot spot in sharding?
options: One shard receiving disproportionately more traffic
The fastest shard in the cluster

hook.text: A user places an order. Instead of calling 5 services in sequence, one event triggers them all in parallel.

buildup.text: Event-driven systems publish events to a bus. Interested services subscribe and react independently.

discovery.text: This decouples services. The order service doesn't need to know about shipping, billing, or notifications.

twist.text: Debugging is harder. When something fails, tracing across async events requires distributed tracing tools.

climax.text: Event-driven architecture enables loose coupling and high scalability at the cost of observability.

punchline.text: Events decouple services — at the cost of visibility.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of event-driven architecture?
options: Services are decoupled and react independently

hook.text: What if you used one database model for writing data and a completely different one for reading it?

buildup.text: CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation — splits the write model from the read model.

discovery.text: Writes go to a normalized, transactional store. Reads come from a denormalized, query-optimized view.

twist.text: The two models must stay in sync, usually through events. Eventual consistency is inherent.

climax.text: CQRS is powerful for systems with very different read and write patterns, but overkill for simple apps.

punchline.text: Optimize reads and writes separately.

quiz.question: What does CQRS stand for?

hook.text: You update your API. Thousands of apps using the old version break overnight.

buildup.text: API versioning lets you evolve your interface without breaking existing clients.

discovery.text: Common strategies: URL versioning (/v1/users), header versioning, or query parameter versioning.

twist.text: Supporting multiple versions means maintaining multiple codepaths. Technical debt grows with each version.

climax.text: Versioning buys backward compatibility but demands a clear deprecation strategy to stay manageable.

punchline.text: New features without breaking old clients.

quiz.question: Why is API versioning important?
options: It lets you evolve APIs without breaking existing clients

hook.text: You need to add a column to a table with 500 million rows. One wrong move and the site goes down.

buildup.text: Database migrations are versioned scripts that evolve the schema over time, safely and repeatably.

discovery.text: Good migrations are backward-compatible: add before remove, never rename in one step.

twist.text: Large table migrations can lock the database for minutes. Online migration tools avoid downtime.

climax.text: Schema evolution is inevitable. The discipline of safe migrations keeps systems alive during change.

punchline.text: Change the schema without stopping the system.

quiz.question: What is a backward-compatible migration?
options: A change that doesn't break existing code or queries
Rolling back to a previous version

hook.text: Netflix deploys new code to production but only 1% of users see the new feature. That's a feature flag.

buildup.text: Feature flags wrap new functionality in an if-statement controlled by a configuration, not code.

discovery.text: Teams can deploy code daily and gradually roll out features, rolling back instantly if something breaks.

twist.text: Stale feature flags accumulate as technical debt. Without cleanup, codebases become tangled with dead branches.

climax.text: Feature flags decouple deployment from release, giving teams speed and safety simultaneously.

punchline.text: Deploy daily, release when you're ready.

quiz.question: What do feature flags decouple?

hook.text: You have two identical production environments: blue is live, green has the new version.

buildup.text: You deploy the update to green, test it thoroughly, then switch the load balancer to point at green.

discovery.text: If something goes wrong, switching back to blue is instant — no rollback required.

twist.text: Running two full environments doubles infrastructure cost during the transition window.

climax.text: Blue-green deployments trade cost for confidence: zero-downtime releases with instant rollback.

punchline.text: Two environments, zero downtime, instant rollback.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of blue-green deployments?
options: Zero downtime with instant rollback capability

hook.text: Netflix intentionally kills random servers in production. They call it Chaos Monkey.

buildup.text: In distributed systems, failures are inevitable. Designing for failure means assuming things will break.

discovery.text: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and fallbacks keep the system running when parts fail.

twist.text: Systems that never fail in testing fail catastrophically in production. Chaos engineering prevents surprises.

climax.text: Resilient systems don't prevent failures — they survive them gracefully and recover automatically.

punchline.text: Don't prevent failure — survive it gracefully.

quiz.question: What is Netflix's Chaos Monkey?
options: A tool that intentionally kills random servers in production
